items.title: From Eyeballs to Annual Run Rates (ARR): Buzzy Pricing Metrics and the Anthropic Trade!
items.content:
I was in San Francisco last week to talk to NYU Stern Alumni on October 15, and it was the day that Anthropic had a pre-IPO meeting with prospective investors. While I was not at the meeting, the focus  of teh gathering was laying a foundation for its upcoming IPO, with the company reporting third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, which news reports described as surging 45% over the previous quarter's revenues, and positive profits, albeit on an adjusted basis. During the meeting, Anthropic also reported an annual revenue run rate (ARR) of $67 billion, a metric that those in the AI space have adopted with gusto, with an estimate that the ARR would exceed $100 billion by the end of the year. The nature of ARR, where choices on how revenue is calculated (gross versus net) and on annualization periods (daily, weekly or monthly) can make a significant difference, has led investors to be skeptical about comparing these numbers across time and companies.  While I share some of that skepticism, it is worth remembering that young businesses are often priced on inventive metrics, some with more basis than others. In the late nineties, dot.com companies were priced not just on the number of visitors to their websites, but on eyeballs , where Mary Meeker argued that ad spending at these companies was correlated with time that these visitors spent on websites (eyeballs), rather than with total visitors. In the last decade, you saw social media companies priced based upon the number of users and subscription-based companies on subscriber numbers. In this post, I will try to lay out the rationale for why pricing supplants valuation in young companies and why that pricing almost always has to be built around messy metrics like eyeballs, users and ARR, rather than more conventional metrics like earnings, book value or cash flows.

 Young Companies in a Corporate Life Cycle 
      All businesses, no matter how large and established they might be today, started as young businesses and matured. With that perspective in mind, I will start this discussion by placing young businesses in a corporate life cycle in the figure below:

One of the first steps in analyzing a company is placing it in the right stage of the life cycle, and there are three choices that you can use in making this placement:
 Chronological age : The first and simplest choice is to look at the age of a business, putting companies that have been in operation for short periods into the young company grouping and classifying those that have been in operation for longer as mature. While this approach is easy to use, and for the most part, effective, it can be misleading in businesses like infrastructure, where it can take decades to get established, and in technology, where the lack of capital intensity can allow a company can go from start-up to mature in a few years. Industry grouping : Another choice is categorizing industry groups into life cycle stages and assuming that any company that belongs to a specific industry group shares its life cycle characteristics. For decades, investors have viewed technology as a shorthand for growth and put technology companies into the earlier stages of the life cycle and utilities as mature or even declining and put all utility companies into the mature to declining company grouping. The limitation of this approach is that there will be divergence within each group, where some companies separate themselves from their industry group; there are mature and even declining companies that are in the technology grouping, and there are power companies that have taken advantage of the data center boom to become growth companies. With technology in particular, where companies age in dog years, I talked about how companies can get mis-categorized and sometimes mismanaged as growth companies , even though their best days are behind them.  Operating metrics : Ultimately, life cycle effects show up in the operating metrics of companies, and there are common characteristics that young companies share, and they include the following: High revenue growth : Young companies usually have high revenue growth, and while this is usually off a small revenue base, there are exceptions, where companies with scaled up revenues are still able to show high growth. Operating losses : As young companies scale up, they usually struggle with unformed business models, and at low scale, their fixed costs overwhelm their revenues, resulting in negative or very low operating profit margins. Negative free cash flows : Free cash flows are after reinvestment, and as young companies invest to deliver on their potential growth, that reinvestment will generate negative free cash flows. Failure risk : The confluence of small revenues, losses and negative free cashflows, which must be funded with external capital (equity or debt) exposes young firms to significant risk of failure. The figure below captures the shifts in operating metrics, as companies move through the life cycle:

 Put simply, if a company has revenue growth in single digits, stable margins and positive free cash flows to the firm, it is a mature company, no matter how it views itself. Conversely, a firm with high revenue growth, negative or very low profit margins and large negative free cashflows to the firms is a young growth firm, no matter what its scale. Recognizing those characteristics is critical in understanding why so many give up on valuing young companies, and why pricing will often be based on unfamiliar metrics.

     How do Anthropic and OpenAI measure up in the life cycle? Using a patchwork of public data and leaked information, here are the numbers on key operating metrics that I have as of October 2026 for both companies: 

 The sky-high revenue growth and operating losses are a clear indication that these are young, growth companies, but note that the revenues (albeit on an ARR basis) at both companies are already large, suggesting that they are growing at scale. That should come as no surprise, since they are both rumored to be looking at IPOs in excess of a trillion dollars, in terms of total market capitalization. The business models are still in flux in both companies, as they wrestle with how best to structure their business models (usage versus subscription) and struggle with market targeting questions (premium versus mass market). I know that Anthropic claimed to be profitable in the second quarter of 2026, but I don't think that even Anthropic believes this to be true, since these are adjusted profits and the adjustments represent a patchwork of add-backs of legitimate expenses. As for cash flows, both Anthropic and OpenAI are deep in the hole, with negative free cash flows, at the moment, and whether they are able to generate positive cash flows in the future is entirely a function of how the AI business evolves over time.

 Pricing versus Valuation: Across the life cycle 
     I will start with a distinction that I believe needs to be made between two approaches to attaching numbers to assets and businesses. The first is to value that asset or business, based on its capacity to generate and grow cash flows, and the risk in those cashflows, i.e., intrinsic valuation. The second is to price that asset or business by looking at what others are paying for "similar' assets, thus reducing pricing to demand and supply. The picture below captures that difference:

 It is true that if you believed in efficient markets, price would converge on value, but if you did, you would save yourself the time and aggravation associated with trying to price or value assets by investing in index funds, and moving on to more productive pursuits. If you don't believe in efficient markets, you can take one of two paths. You can take the investor route ,  trying to value assets and businesses, with the intent of buying undervalued and/or selling overvalued companies, and hoping that price converges on value. Alternatively, you can take the trading path , where you throw up your hands on intrinsic value, arguing that it is too subjective and difficult to estimate, and make your money by buying investments at low prices and selling them at higher prices,  using whatever tools (including charts and technical indicators) you want to use, to make your judgments. 
     While you can value and price any business, there are reasons why the usage of each can vary depending upon where a company is in the life cycle. To value a business, you have to estimate expected future cash flows, and to make these estimates of cash flows, growth and risk, and you generally draw on three sources of information: 

 Financial statements : The current financial statements of a company provide information on unit economics, profitability and risk, and historical financial statements are useful in assessing growth in the business and changes in business profitability. For mature businesses that have been in operating for long period, much or even all of what you need to value the company can be in its financial statements, but for younger companies, the current financials may not yield much (as growth and unformed business models create noise) and there is little history, Market size and growth : Knowing the size of the total market that a company is aiming for, and how quickly it is growing can help put reasonability constraints on the growth rate and market you estimate for a company. For companies in established markets, this should be relatively easy to do, but for companies in new and evolving markets, this can become difficult. Industry statistics : As you forecast profit margins and the risk profile for a company, having that information for the crosssection of companies in the industry can establish bounds and help in making estimates. If you frame an intrinsic valuation in terms of the big estimation questions that need to be addressed to arrive at value, starting with the cash flows from existing investments, moving on to estimating the value that will be added by future growth and assessing risk, you can see that valuing young companies will always be more complicated than valuing more mature businesses. In fact, looking at Anthropic and OpenAI, you can see why valuation will be daunting:

 While I am a glutton for punishment, and I will try, albeit with error, to make my best judgments on Anthropic's future cash flows, risk and value (as I did with SpaceX), when the prospectus is made public, I understand why most will turn away in the face of uncertainty and choose not to value the company. Some of these investors will also look at how those that they believe know more about that companies are assessing its value, and peruse prior venture capital rounds at both Anthropic and OpenAI for clues on value.  Both Anthropic and OpenAI have been active in raising equity as private companies, and the most recent rounds yield estimates of what these private investors thought they were worth, at least at the time the capital was raised. The table below summarizes the number of VC rounds, with capital raised, at both companies, as well as the pricing in their most recent rounds:

 Anthropic's VC round in May 2026 , from a cross section of big-name venture capitalists, raised $65 billion for the company, at a post-money pricing of $965 billion .   OpenAI's most recent capital raise was in March 2026, when it raised $122 billion, at a post-money pricing for the company at $852 billion . OpenAI also has a pending round of capital raise ahead of an IPO, where they expect to raise $30 billion with a pricing for the company of roughly $1.4 trillion .  

      While you may be tempted to assume that the VC pricing in these rounds are rooted in value, venture capitalists are in the pricing game, as I have argued in prior posts , In fact, they, stretch pricing metrics and definitions of peer groups, and VC valuation is almost always forward pricing :

 In the case of Anthropic and OpenAI, this forward pricing process is both more compressed and even less informative than at most young companies, with investors viewing the companies as imminent IPOs, and pricing them based upon their expectations of the pricing of the public offering, and discounting that expected price for negative surprises about the company's prospects that may lower the pricing or delay/cancel the IPO:

 The expected pricing will be a function of pricing in prior VC rounds, management wishlists and even rumors, and the discount applied will increase as the time to the IPO lengthens and with the uncertainties about the company and its potential market. For Anthropic, for instance, at the time of the VC round, the expected pricing for the IPO was $1.15 trillion, well below what the expectations are today, and reflective of how much can change over short periods with young companies, and the $965 billion pricing in the VC round would have represented a $150 billion discount on the estimate.

 Pricing Process 
      While the reluctance to value young companies, and fall back to pricing is understandable, I would push back on the notion that doing so dispenses with the need to make the assumptions about cashflows, growth and risk that are required in intrinsic valuation. In this section, I will break down the pricing process into steps, and look at the issues that you faced when valuing these companies also create impediments in pricing, and in the next section, why using a multiple of annualized revenue run rates (ARR) or even eyeballs makes implicit assumptions about future profitability, growth and reinvestment. 

 The Steps in the Process 
     If, in pricing, you attach a number to an asset or business, based upon what others are paying for similar assets or business, how exactly does this process play out when valuing a company or business? No matter who does the pricing, and how sophisticated they claim to be, there are three steps in pricing companies:

 Standardize the price : The nature of pricing shares in public markets is that the share price is a function of share count, which is arbitrary; a stock split for instance halves the price while doubling the count and total market capitalization or value is a function of company size. To allow for comparisons across companies, you standardize the market price by dividing by a common variable that you can obtain for each of the companies in your comparison, with the choices ranging from revenues (or revenue drivers) to earnings to cashflow variants to book value. Since the market price can be for just equity (market capitalization) or for the entire business (enterprise value, which includes net debt), the denominator has to be defined in the same terms, with equity (operating) income and book value of equity (invested capital) going with market capitalization (enterprise value). Find peer group companies : For pricing to be functional, you have to find other priced companies just like the one that you are pricing. The simplistic solution is to start with other companies in the same industry or business grouping, with added constraints on geography and company size thrown in. Needless to say, even if done with care, the choice of companies in the peer group is subjective and can vary across analysts and investors, even when looking at the same company. Control for differences : No mater what pricing metric (PE, EV to Sales etc.) you pick, there will be fundamental reasons why companies will trade at different values, and for a pricing to have substance, you have to control for differences. Thus, if PE ratio is your metric, a company that expects higher growth in earnings or lower risk than its peer group, should trade at a higher PE ratio than the peer group does, and that difference has to enter your discussion. The picture below captures these steps, with the variants on pricing metrics and the considerations in peer group construction included:

 While this process remains the same for every pricing, there are reasons why pricing metrics will vary across companies and why peer group construction may be easier in some cases than other, and I will take Anthropic and OpenAI through the process.

1. Pricing metrics 
     With some companies, your choice of pricing metrics will span the spectrum, with revenues, earnings, cash flows and book value all competing as scalars. However, your choices will narrow at others, and one reason that is relevant to the Anthropic/OpenAI discussion is where a company falls in the life cycle:

 As you can see, early in the life cycle, when companies are losing money, have negative free cashflows and little tangible capital invested in assets in place, you will see revenue often as the only viable metric, leading to revenue multiples dominating the discourse. Put simply, desperation drives you up the income statement until you find a positive number. It should be no surprise, therefore, that the metric that companies and investors have focused on with Anthropic and OpenAI is revenues . Those revenues are growing so quickly at these companies, that their argument is that trailing numbers are dated by the time hey are released, and that has led to the shift to annualized revenue run rates (where using revenues from the last week or month allows for more updated vales). As we noted earlier, the perils with annualized revenue rates (ARR) is that they are not standardized and can be easily gamed. Just in the last few weeks, there have been news stories on the divergence between gross and net revenues with OpenAI shifting towards using the latter, lowering ARR from $70 billion to $50 billion, while Anthropic continues to report gross revenues and the cloud provider payments as expenses. In addition, you can compute ARR using the last day's, the last week's and the last month's revenues, and while Anthropic and OpenAI have both converged on monthly annualization, there is nothing that binds them to continue to do so. 

     There is a second choice that will come into play as the debate about Anthropic's pricing becomes more heated, and that is whether to use revenues in a future period, i.e.. forward revenue . By forecasting the annualized revenue run rate of $100 billion plus by the end of 2026, Anthropic has already opened the door, but do not be surprised if investors and analysts shift to looking at revenues in 2030 or 2036, since scaling prices today to forward revenues five or ten years out will make the pricing multiple look lower, and thus more defensible. Once you decide to go forward in time, it is plausible that you can even shift to expected earnings in 2031 or 2036, built around expected operating or net profit margins; arguing that Anthropic is cheap because it trades (today) at 25 times 2036 earnings (based on your estimated revenues and net margins) brings the multiple back to earth, but at what cost? Investors use frames of what comprises normal or high, based  upon their acquaintance with a multiple, and many will (mistakenly) compare these forwards earnings multiples to current earnings multiples in the market to make their investment judgment on cheap or expensive. 
     There is a third choice, and that is to relate the pricing of these companies to a variable that you believe will be correlated with future revenues and earnings. With that choice, you can see the rationale for estimating enterprise value per user or subscriber for user and subscriber based companies, with the connector being the logic that more users and subscribers today is a leading indicator of higher revenues and earnings in the future. It was that logic that led Mary Meeker and other internet analysts to use website visitors and eyeballs in pricing dot com companies, and while you may disagree, the logic holds. With OpenAI and Anthropic, where the power, reach and revenues of AI agents is dependent on having access to compute power, you could scale the market cap and enterprise value at these compani

items.title: Stock Prices, Earnings and Cashflows: The AI Effect plays through!
items.content:
In a post at the end of August 2026, I talked about interest rates in 2026 and marveled at the capacity of equities to keep rising in the face of rising rates. I argued that the resilience of stocks during the year could be traced to higher-than-expected earnings being reported by companies in 2026, and a concurrent increase in expected earnings in 2027 and 2028. Now that September 2026 is one for the record books, it is time to take stock and dig a little deeper, especially since the month brought about one of the largest increase in treasury yield rates in recent memory, and stock prices still held their own. In particular, I want to examine the earnings at US companies, in the aggregate and by sector, trying to trace out where the earnings increase is coming from, and how that increased earnings is playing out on corporate balance sheets and cash flows.
 Stock Prices and Rates 
 In my earlier post on interest rates, I had looked at treasury rates by day through the end of August, and I will begin this section by updating that chart to include a tumultuous September:

 I had described the rise in rates between January and August as gradual, but the rise in rates in September was anything but, as the ten-year rate rose from 4.75% at the start of the month to 5.29% at the end. In fact, to put the 54 basis point rise in the ten-year rate in context, take a look at the distribution of monthly rate changes in the ten-year treasury in the chart below:

 The September rise in rates would put in the top ten percent of 770 monthly rate changes that we have seen between 1962 and 2026. In the face of the mark up in rates, stocks held their own in September, at least in the aggregate, and you can see that in the chart below, where I look at aggregate market values, by month, and by sector:
 = 
 The market added $2.5 trillion in market capitalization across all stocks in September 2026, but almost $1.5 trillion of that came from technology As you look across the entire year, broken down by quarters, here is what you see in the aggregate market caps:
 Only companies listed at the start of 2026 included I excluded firms that were not listed at the start of 2026 from the list since including them will give a misleading sense of returns to investors; adding SpaceX, for instance, which was listed in June 2026, will increase the value of communication service companies by more than $2 trillion, but it was listed at roughly that value. There are many who have pointed to the fact that US equities, while up for the year, have seen divergence in performance, and you can see that phenomenon play out in two statistics. The first is that three sectors - technology, energy and materials have carried the market, with technology being the biggest contributor to market gains. The second is that the percent of companies within each sector that are up for the year is about 50% across the market, and in the third quarter, about 65% of all listed stocks saw dropping stock prices.
     It is often difficult to make sense of what is moving stock prices because there are so many factors from growth to interest rates to cash payout that are pulling in different directions. It is to counter this confusion that I have resorted to estimating an i mplied equity risk premium , where I estimate the internal rate of return you can earn by buying equities, given how they are priced, and their expected earnings growth and cash flows, as well as  interest rates. That calculation, which I have done at the start of each month since September 2008, yields an expected return of 8.99% for equities and an equity risk premium of 3.70% (3.92%) over the ten-year treasury rate (dollar riskfree rate) of 5.29% (5.07%) at the start of October 2026:  

 Note that this estimation is model-agnostic and is an internal rate of return for investing in stocks, given expectations of the cash flows from investing in equities. If you are a market timer, and I am not one, you could use this implied equity risk premium as a barometer of market priciness, with a lower number indicating overpricing and a higher number indicating underpricing. 
 Download spreadsheet 

 The jump in US treasury rates in September 2026 has had an effect, with the equity risk premium dropping below 4% for the first time this year.  In fact, even as the ten-year treasury rate has climbed this year from 4.18% to 5.29%, the expected return on stocks has also gone up from 8.41% at the start of 2026 to 8.99% on September 30, 2026.
 The AI Cap Ex Boom: Accounting and Corporate Finance Consequences 
     The focus on stock prices and interest rates can sometimes distract us from paying attention to corporate investing, financing and cash return policies that drive value. It should not surprise you, given the times we live in, that AI is at the heart of the business story that is driving corporate behavior, and in the process, providing the fodder for market resistance to higher rates. I will begin with an assessment of how the trillions of dollars in AI cap ex will show up in financial statements:

 As you can see, the AI cap ex story is a complicated one, if you are looking at market aggregates, because the market includes both the companies that are spending the money building the AI architecture, which includes data centers and other infrastructure, as well as the companies that are supplying the ingredients for that infrastructure. 

 The builders of the architecture are the hyperscalers (Meta, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft et al.), and the money they spend on cap ex will cause lower earnings, at least until the cap ex starts paying off, in the form of amortization of the AI cap ex, as well as a hit to their free cash flows, which are after cap ex.  The money spent on AI cap ex though becomes revenues to the chip makers (Nvidia and TSMC leading the way), network equipment manufacturers (Broadcom, Micron and Marvel, to name just three), power plant builders (Constellation Energy et al.) and even real estate developers focused on data centers (Equinix, Digital Realty), and ultimately net profits (with net margins driving the bottom line).  It is true that there are gray zones here, with some AI builders also  benefiting from being suppliers (Amazon is spending money on AI cap ex but is also benefiting from the usage of its cloud space for data storage, and Nvidia, while selling the chips that go into the architecture, is also investing directly or indirectly into data centers).  
     As we trace through the aggregated effects of the AI cap ex boom on accounting statements, there are two caveats that need to be stated up front. The first is that the data that is accessible to the public, and which I will be using, will be data from publicly traded companies . To the extent that some of AI's big players (builders and suppliers) are private, I will be missing the revenues, earnings, cash flows and invested capital at these large private players (which include at least two companies in Anthropic and OpenAI that are expected to command trillion dollar plus market caps. The second is that some of the AI cap ex is taking the form of j oint ventures and off-balance sheet entities , and the accounting for these (especially on the debt side) may not fully reflect the consequences for firms. As a result, the numbers you see in the public company financials will understate the full effect across all businesses. 
      With those caveats in place, the business story for US equities starts with massive capital expenditures in AI , with trillions being invested into data centers and AI architecture. It is true that this cap ex is top heavy, with the top ten hyper-scalers accounting for more than $2 trillion of the AI cap ex, but in the table below, I look at the aggregate cap ex reported in corporate financial statements at all publicly traded companies in the United States:

 Even with the caveats about understatement, but you can still see that cap ex in the second quarter of 2026, which is our last completed quarter of reported financials, was up $133.4 billion from the cap ex in the second quarter of 2025, an increase of almost 36%. Again, the surge in cap ex is concentrated, with technology, communication services and consumer discretionary all registering growth of more than 50% in the quarter-to-quarter comparison. 
     Accounting incorporates capital expenditures into the balance sheet as assets, and reflects how this cap ex is funded (debt or equity) by increasing the book values of the funding used in the investment . A surge in cap ex, such as the one that we have seen in 2026, will show up as higher book values for equity, debt and invested capital, and we capture this effect, by sector, in the table below: 

 Across all US stocks, the book equity has increased almost 13%, between the second quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, and total debt is up almost 8%. In dollar terms, the book equity at US companies increased by $1.8 trillion between the second quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026, and book debt by $1.9 trillion, over the same  period.  Technology, being the most active player in AI cap ex, has seen much bigger increases in both numbers, with book equity rising almost 30% and total debt up about 18.8%. 
     From an earnings perspective, the focus on cap ex and book values may seem misplaced, since the former can only decrease cash flows and the latter impacts accounting returns. In 2026, though, the increased capital expenditures on AI are affecting earnings for a simple reason. The money spent on cap ex by a company building AI architecture will become revenues (and earnings) for other companies that supply the building blocks for the architecture . There is a reason why Nvidia has been the biggest beneficiary from the AI cap ex boom so far, since its chips, marked up massively, power the data centers, and there others, from electrical equipment makers to power companies to real estate developers who have also reaped the benefits. It is true that there should be increased amortization expenses at the AI builders , but the longer amortization schedules being used by many of them is reducing the current hit to earnings at these companies. The earnings effect of the AI story can be seen in the table below, where I look at aggregate net income at US companies, broken down by sector:

 Note that in both the first and second quarters of 2026, US companies have seen earnings surge over the corresponding quarters in 2025, with aggregate earnings increasing from $511 billion to $692 billion (translating into an earnings growth rate of 35%, quarter-to-quarter) in the first quarter of 2026 and from $576 billion to $904 billion (translating into an earnings growth rate of 57%, quarter-to-quarter) in the second quarter of 2026. As with stock prices, the earnings benefits are not broad-based, with more than half of all companies in the market reporting declines in net income, and there are wide differences in earnings growth across sectors. Technology, financials and communication services have seen the biggest increases in earnings, and health care, utilities and real estate have lagged.
     A cap-ex driven surge in aggregate earnings comes with an asterisk, since the higher earnings across firms will be partially or even fully offset by capital expenditures across firms, leading to free cashflows to firms  often growing at much lower rates than earnings. Since these free cash flows are what fund dividend payments and stock buybacks, I looked at cash returned to shareholders in both forms in 2026: 

 In the aggregate, dividends in the last twelve months are up about $43.3 billion (about 5%) from dividends in the 2025 calendar year, and stock buybacks are up about $106.7 billion (about 9%). In fact, if you net out stock issuances, which spiked in the second quarter of 2026, from buybacks, net buybacks have grown bout 7% between the last calendar year and now. Those numbers represent reasonable step ups from the last year's numbers, but they clearly have not kept up with the earnings growth in 2026. One way to see the disconnect that is occurring between earnings and cash flows is to look at the cash returned as a percent of earnings for the S&P 500 companies over time:

 For much of the last two decades, US companies have returned 80% or more, and sometimes more than 100% of their earnings, to shareholders in dividends and buybacks. Starting in about 2024, you can see a divergence with earnings rising much faster than cash returns, and in the last twelve months leading into 2026, the companies in the S&P 500 returned 63% of their earnings to shareholders , a low not seen since 2004. Many of those who were criticizing US companies for buying back too much stock and not investing enough back into businesses are now finding fault with those same companies scaling back buybacks and investing more into AI cap ex, leading to the conclusion that these critics will find fault no matter what companies do. 
 The AI Business Resolution: Accounting and Market Consequences 
      It is true that the massive investments in AI cap ex are being driven by expectations that AI as a business will enjoy not only a large market, but one where the winners can sustain huge profits for the long term. As I noted in my post on AI as a business , this is a plausible path, but there are vast disagreements on whether this is the expected one, given uncertainties about all three layers of the business story - the size of the total addressable market, the unit economics/operating margins of companies in the business and the moats and competitive advantages that will allow for sustainability in profits. In effect, the only point on which you have a consensus on is that companies have collectively invested a huge amount in AI cap ex, and the point at which AI optimists and pessimists is diverge is on what the payoffs from that investment will be, with optimists arguing that AI will deliver on expectations and that the profits that will be generated by AI cap ex investors in the future will be sufficient to earn returns on that investment that exceed the cost of capital, and pessimists positing that this is wishful thinking, and that the profits from AI, even if considerable, will not be large enough to justify the up front investments. It is also worth remembering that determining which side is closer to the truth will not be made by looking at arguments about annualized revenue run rates at Anthropic and OpenAI today, but will require waiting for the AI product and service market to gain substance. Waiting does not come easily to any of us, and there will be premature claims of victory from both sides, often based upon paltry evidence and incomplete information.
      So, what will the accounting and market consequences be, if the AI pathway diverges from expectations? In the table below, I trace out the accounting and market consequences of the AI business working better than expected at delivering growth and profits, as well as if i does much worse than expected:

 In the best case scenarios for AI, the companies that have invested in AI, at least collectively, will be able to deliver not just earnings growth from the cap ex, but enough incremental earnings to generate returns on the AI cap ex that exceed their cost of capital for those investments.  Their lenders will be made whole, with interest and principal payments, and the AI builders will see their cashflows  become more positive,  but the companies, while successful, will emerge as very different businesses than when they entered the space, more capital intensive than they used to be.  In the worst case scenarios for AI, there will be both accounting and market carnage, as accountants write off large portions of the AI cap ex, because of its failure to deliver promised profits, and while cash flows may recover, markets will correct the pricing of these companies to reflect a lack of trust in management. For companies that were excessively dependent on debt for their AI cap ex, there will be defaults and increased distress, with lenders feeling the pain as well.  There are also intermediate scenarios, ranging from AI being a moderate success, where the companies investing AI may be able to extract some earnings from their investment, but not enough to cover the cost of capital, to a moderate failure, where some companies may be able to justify their investments and most will not.
     Given that AI business surprises will have both market and accounting consequences, I will hazard a guess that the market will lead in this process and accounting will follow. In short, if AI is working better (worse) than expected, you should see stock prices at AI-centered businesses rise (fall) before you see accountants respond. Put simply, in the event that AI does not deliver on its promise, waiting to act until accountants write off AI cap ex to sell your AI company implies that you waited too long. 

 An Investor Perspective: Taking Stock and Taking Action 
     In my post on AI as a business, I zeroed in on the debate between AI optimists, pointing to huge (albeit unspecified) markets for AI products and services, and AI skeptics, drawing attention to the outsized capital expenditures. While that debate plays out, financial markets and businesses cannot afford to wait for resolution, and are acting now, with companies making investments in cap ex and markets building in their expectations of what that will mean for future earnings into stock prices. That has made not just the market but also the economy a giant bet on AI, with success vindicating the companies and investors who have bet on it, and failure manifesting in massive write offs at companies (feeding into losses) and stock price markdowns.  As investors, there are four choices that you can make, and unfortunately, none of these choices give you the luxury of sitting out the AI debate:

 Go all in on the AI story winning (and doing it soon) : The first betis that AI is an unstoppable force, destined to change the way we live and work, with AI businesses reaping the benefits of the disruption. It is a plausible story, albeit one that raises significant questions about the economic and social costs of disruption, with disagreements about the speed and extent of the disruption. It was the story that Leo Aschenbrenner built Situational Awareness around, and while excessive leverage, driven by hubris and over-conviction, brought him down, it is possible that you could mimic his strategy, of buying the AI disruptors and/or selling the AI disrupted, albeit with far less leverage, and win in the long term. Go with the market consensus : In an age where we worship at the altar of crowd wisdom in almost everything we do, you could examine what the market is pricing in, as its AI story, and go along. At the moment, at least, the market seems to be building in the expectation that AI will be a major disruption that will give rise to large and valuable businesses and it is picking its winners among the AI architecture companies (with Nvidia the biggest so far) and among the LLMs (SpaceX in the public markets and OpenAI and Anthropic in the private markets). For better or worse, you may have already chosen this path implicitly, if your pension funds and savings are invested passively, getting partial exposure to this story with an S&P 500 fund, and more complete exposure if you buy a total market fund for US equities.  Be an AI skeptic : There are many reasons to be skeptical about the AI story, and for some, that skepticism may lead to the belief that AI will not make it as a viable business, or at least one large enough to sustain the pricing and investment you are seeing for it.
